slides.heading: A rare line-up
slides.text: In the late 1970s, the giant outer planets lined up in a way that happens only about once every 175 years. A spacecraft could visit them one after another!

slides.heading: Planet slingshots
slides.text: Flying close to a planet lets its gravity swing a spacecraft round and throw it onwards, faster. It's called a gravity assist, and it saves years of travel.

slides.heading: A tour of the giants
slides.text: Here is NASA's picture of the planets and moons the two Voyager spacecraft visited. Voyager 1 would fly past Jupiter and Saturn, then head for the stars.

image.alt: A montage of the planets and moons the Voyagers visited

slides.heading: Your mission
slides.text: Find the launch window, make the Golden Record, fly past Jupiter and Saturn, and travel all the way out of the Sun's bubble, into interstellar space!

intro: Planets move around the Sun at different speeds. To visit Jupiter AND Saturn, Voyager had to leave when both would be in just the right place by the time it got there!
launchWindow.doneLine: 1977: the perfect window! A line-up like this happens only about once every 175 years. Voyager 2's path even carried on to Uranus and Neptune: the Grand Tour!
launchWindow.resultText: Space missions wait for launch windows: times when the planets are in just the right places.

task.title: Line up the planets!
task.help: Slide the year until Jupiter and Saturn sit in the yellow circles.

readyTask.title: Lined up!
readyTask.help: Both planets are in place. Press Launch!

intro: The Golden Record is a message from Earth, in case anyone out there ever finds Voyager. A team led by astronomer Carl Sagan chose what to put on it.

items.name: Hello in 55 languages
items.info: Greetings in 55 languages, from ancient ones to modern ones.

items.name: Whale songs
items.info: Humpback whale songs: a hello from another kind of animal.

items.name: Thunder and rain
items.info: The sounds of nature: thunder, wind, rain, waves and more.

items.name: A baby crying
items.info: The sounds of people: a baby crying, laughter, footsteps and a heartbeat.

items.name: Rock and roll music
items.info: 90 minutes of music from all over the world, from Bach and Beethoven to Chuck Berry's 'Johnny B. Goode'.

items.name: A kiss
items.info: Yes, really: the sound of a kiss is on the record!

items.name: 115 pictures
items.info: Pictures of people, animals, cities, food and our planet, stored as sound on the record.

items.name: A map to find Earth
items.info: The cover has a map that uses pulsars, spinning stars, to show where our Sun is.

items.name: A dinosaur bone
items.why: The record only holds sounds and pictures, not real objects.

items.name: A pizza
items.why: No food on board! It would never last billions of years.

items.name: A video game
items.why: There are no games on it. Home video games were brand new in 1977!

goldenRecord.doneLine: That's Earth's greatest hits! The records are made of gold-plated copper, and they should last a billion years or more out in space.
goldenRecord.resultText: If anyone out there ever finds Voyager, the Golden Record will tell them who we are.

task.title: Fill the Golden Record!
task.help: Drag the things that are really on it onto the record.

intro: An alien wouldn't know how to play a record! So the cover has instructions, drawn in pictures and science instead of words.
recordCover.wrong: Not that one! Look at the shapes again.
recordCover.doneLine: You read the cover! Even billions of years from now, a clever alien could work out how to play the record and where it came from.
recordCover.resultText: Scientists wrote the instructions in maths and science, because they hoped those would be the same everywhere in the universe.

task.title: Read the cover!
task.help: Drag each meaning onto the drawing it explains.

meanings.name: How to play the record
meanings.info: The record and its needle, seen from above and from the side, and how long one turn should take.

meanings.name: How to see the pictures
meanings.info: These wavy lines explain how to turn sounds back into pictures, line by line, like an old TV.

meanings.name: Where Earth is
meanings.info: Lines to 14 pulsars, spinning stars that flash like lighthouses, point to our Sun.

meanings.name: A clock for the whole universe
meanings.info: Two hydrogen atoms. Hydrogen is everywhere, so a tiny flip it makes can be a unit of time any scientist would understand.

voyagerReveal.title: Voyager 1
voyagerReveal.subtitle: A robot explorer about the size of a small car

stats.label: Dish antenna
stats.value: 3.7 m (12 feet) wide, always pointed at Earth

stats.label: Power
stats.value: 3 nuclear batteries that turn heat into electricity

stats.label: Computer memory
stats.value: About 69 kilobytes: less than one phone photo

voyagerReveal.line: Meet Voyager 1! Its big dish talks to Earth, and its long arms keep the instruments away from the rest of the spacecraft. Drag to spin it, then let's launch!

slides.heading: Liftoff!
slides.text: Voyager 1 launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on a Titan-Centaur rocket.

image.alt: The Titan-Centaur rocket carrying Voyager 1 lifting off

slides.heading: Two Voyagers
slides.text: Its twin, Voyager 2, had launched first, on August 20. But Voyager 1 took a faster path, so it would reach Jupiter first.

slides.heading: Looking back
slides.text: On its way out, Voyager 1 took the first ever picture of Earth and the Moon together in one frame, from more than 11 million km (7 million miles) away.

image.alt: A crescent Earth and a crescent Moon in one picture

slides.credit: Photo: NASA/JPL · Earth and Moon, by Voyager 1

slides.heading: Next stop: Jupiter
slides.text: It took about 18 months to reach Jupiter. Time to get the cameras ready!

intro: March 1979: Voyager 1 is racing past Jupiter, the biggest planet of all! Its cameras sit on a moving platform, and you're in charge of pointing them.
flyby.missed: Missed it! Wait until the frame turns green, then snap.

targets.name: Great Red Spot
targets.fact: A giant storm bigger than Earth, swirling for more than 150 years.

targets.name: Io
targets.fact: A moon covered in volcanoes! Voyager 1 found the first active volcanoes beyond Earth.

targets.name: Europa
targets.fact: An icy moon covered in cracks. Scientists now think an ocean hides under its ice.

targets.name: Ganymede
targets.fact: The biggest moon in the solar system: it's even bigger than the planet Mercury.

targets.name: Callisto
targets.fact: One of the most cratered places in the whole solar system.

targets.name: Jupiter's ring
targets.fact: A thin, faint ring of dust. Voyager 1 discovered it!

flyby.notEnough: Not enough photos this time. Let's fly past again and try to get more!
flyby.resultText: Voyager 1 sent back thousands of pictures of Jupiter and its moons, showing them up close for the very first time.

task.title: Photograph Jupiter!
task.help: Move the frame onto a yellow target. When it turns green, press SNAP!

intro: Days after passing Jupiter, engineer Linda Morabito was checking a photo of the moon Io. It had been made extra bright on purpose, to show the stars behind it. Then she noticed something strange...
ioPlume.notThere: Nothing there. Try somewhere along the edge of Io.
ioPlume.tooDark: Too dark to see anything! Turn the brightness up first.
ioPlume.found: You found it! It was a giant volcanic plume, about 300 km (190 miles) high: the first erupting volcano ever seen beyond Earth!
ioPlume.resultText: Io has hundreds of volcanoes. Jupiter's gravity squeezes and stretches it, which heats it up inside.

brightTask.title: Turn up the brightness!
brightTask.help: Slide the brightness up to see faint things.

findTask.title: Find the volcano cloud!
findTask.help: Look along Io's edge and tap the faint cloud.

slides.heading: The Great Red Spot
slides.text: Voyager 1's photos showed the Great Red Spot swirling like a giant hurricane, with smaller storms spinning around it.

image.alt: Jupiter's Great Red Spot with swirling clouds

slides.credit: Photo: NASA/JPL · The Great Red Spot, by Voyager 1

slides.heading: Volcanoes on Io
slides.text: Here is the real picture: a volcano erupting into space, glowing blue at Io's edge on the left. Io is the most volcanic place in the solar system.

image.alt: Io with a blue volcanic plume rising from its edge

slides.credit: Photo: NASA/JPL · A volcano erupting on Io, by Voyager 1

slides.heading: Slingshot to Saturn
slides.text: Jupiter's gravity flung Voyager 1 onwards, faster, towards Saturn. It arrived in November 1980.

intro: November 1980: Saturn! But Voyager's cameras could only take black-and-white photos. So how did we get colour pictures?
Each colour picture was made from three black-and-white photos, taken through orange, green and blue filters.
colorFilters.wrongMix: Those colours look strange! Match each filter to its colour channel.
colorFilters.falseColor: Fun fact: scientists sometimes mix the channels differently on purpose, called 'false colour', to make hidden details stand out!
colorFilters.resultText: Many space pictures are made this way, even today: black-and-white photos through filters, combined into colour.

task.title: Colour in Saturn!
task.help: Drag each filter photo into a colour box. Orange goes in red.

slides.heading: Saturn up close
slides.text: Voyager 1 found that Saturn's rings are made of thousands of thin ringlets, with strange dark 'spokes' and a twisted outer ring.

image.alt: Saturn and its rings photographed by Voyager 1

slides.heading: Titan's mystery haze
slides.text: Voyager 1 flew close to Titan, Saturn's biggest moon. It found a thick orange haze, mostly nitrogen like Earth's air, hiding the ground below.

image.alt: Titan, a fuzzy orange ball hidden in haze

slides.heading: A fork in the road
slides.text: Flying close to Titan bent Voyager 1's path up and out of the planets' flat plane, so it could never visit Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 2 went there instead, and it is still the only spacecraft ever to visit them.

intro: Voyager talks to Earth through giant dish antennas in California, Spain and Australia, spread around the world. As Earth spins, each dish turns away from Voyager!
dsn.lost: Signal lost! Tap a dish in the green zone.
dsn.notVisible: That dish is facing away from Voyager. Pick one in the green zone!
factLines: Voyager's radio uses about 20 watts, about as much as a fridge light bulb.
The biggest Deep Space Network dishes are 70 m (230 feet) wide, to catch the faint signal.
A message to Voyager 1 now takes almost a whole day to arrive!
dsn.resultText: With three sites spread around the world, one of them can always see Voyager, so it never has to stop talking to us.

task.title: Keep talking to Voyager!
task.help: When your dish leaves the green zone, tap the next dish in the zone.

intro: February 14, 1990. Before its cameras were switched off for good, Voyager 1 turned around for one last look home: a family portrait of the planets!

planets.name: Jupiter
planets.ask: Find Jupiter! It's the biggest, brightest dot.

planets.name: Saturn
planets.ask: Find Saturn! Look for a golden-yellow dot.

planets.name: Venus
planets.ask: Find Venus! It shines brightly, close to the Sun.
planets.fact: Bright Venus, close to the Sun.

planets.name: Uranus
planets.ask: Find Uranus! It's a small blue-green dot.

planets.name: Neptune
planets.ask: Find Neptune! It's a small blue dot, far from the Sun.

planets.name: Earth
planets.ask: Last one: find Earth! It's a pale blue dot, inside a beam of sunlight.
planets.fact: Earth: a tiny pale blue dot, caught in a beam of sunlight.

portrait.doneLine: You found the whole family! Mercury and Mars were lost in the Sun's glare, and Pluto was too small to see. That tiny dot in the sunbeam is Earth, seen from about 6 billion km (3.7 billion miles) away.
portrait.resultText: The real portrait was made from 60 photos. It was the first picture of our solar system taken from outside.
portrait.lookHelp: Drag to look around the sky. Tap the planet when you spot it.

slides.heading: The Pale Blue Dot
slides.text: Here is NASA's real photo, updated in 2020. Earth is the tiny bright speck inside the beam of sunlight, just right of the middle.

image.alt: Earth as a tiny dot inside a beam of scattered sunlight

slides.credit: Image: NASA/JPL-Caltech · Pale Blue Dot Revisited

slides.heading: "That's here. That's home. That's us."
slides.text: Astronomer Carl Sagan asked for this picture. He said that everyone who ever lived, lived on that tiny dot, so we should take care of it, and of each other.
slides.speak: That's here. That's home. That's us. Astronomer Carl Sagan asked for this picture. He said that everyone who ever lived, lived on that tiny dot, so we should take care of it, and of each other.

slides.heading: Cameras off
slides.text: Right after these pictures, Voyager's cameras were switched off to save power and memory for the long journey ahead. They have been off ever since.

intro: November 2023: Voyager 1 suddenly started sending gibberish! Engineers found one broken memory chip, in a computer that is almost 50 years old.
Every change is a radio message that takes almost a day to reach Voyager, so use as few moves as you can!
memoryFix.blocked: That spot won't work. Try a green spot!
memoryFix.stillBroken: Some code is still on the broken chip!
memoryFix.sending: Sending... the message travels for almost a day...
memoryFix.doneLine: It worked! In April 2024, after months of careful work, the team got readable data from Voyager 1 again. You'll see them celebrate in a moment!
memoryFix.resultText: Fixing a 47-year-old computer from 24 billion km away: one of the most amazing repairs ever.

task.title: Rescue the code!
task.help: Drag each piece off the red broken chip into empty memory. Then press Send.

sendTask.title: All safe! Press Send.
sendTask.help: Send the new memory plan to Voyager.

intro: The Sun blows a wind of tiny particles in every direction. It makes a giant bubble around the planets. Where does the bubble end? Let's watch Voyager 1's data as it flies outwards!
heliopause.resultText: Voyager 1 became the first human-made object ever to reach the space between the stars.

task.title: Find the edge of the Sun's bubble!
task.help: Press Edge! when the yellow line drops AND the blue line jumps up, and they stay there.

heliopause.fakeOut: Not yet! The Sun's particles came back. That was a fake-out.
heliopause.tooLate: You waited too long! Let's watch that part again.
heliopause.edgeFound: August 25, 2012: Voyager 1 left the Sun's bubble and entered interstellar space!

slides.heading: Interstellar space
slides.text: Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space, the space between the stars. Watch NASA explain where the edge of the solar system is!

video.credit: Video: NASA Goddard · Where is the edge of the solar system?

slides.heading: The Sun's bubble
slides.text: This picture shows the bubble made by the Sun's wind, and both Voyagers. Voyager 2 crossed out too, in November 2018.

image.alt: The heliosphere bubble with Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 at its edge

slides.credit: Image: NASA/JPL-Caltech · The heliosphere and the two Voyagers

slides.heading: Still talking
slides.text: After the memory fix, the team received readable data from Voyager 1 again. Here is the moment they found out!

video.src: https://images-assets.nasa.gov/video/JPL-20240425-VOYAGEf-0001-Voyager 1 Team Reacts to Receiving Engineering Data From Spacecraft/JPL-20240425-VOYAGEf-0001-Voyager 1 Team Reacts to Receiving Engineering Data From Spacecraft~mobile.mp4
video.credit: Video: NASA/JPL-Caltech · The Voyager team celebrates

slides.heading: A whole day away
slides.text: Voyager 1 is now more than 25 billion km (15 billion miles) away, the farthest human-made object ever. Its radio messages take about a day to reach us. In about 40,000 years it will pass close to another star.

pages.title: Mission report: Voyager 1

stats.label: Distance now
stats.value: More than 25 billion km (15 billion miles)

image.credit: Image: NASA/JPL-Caltech · Voyager and the Golden Record

pages.say: Voyager 1 launched in 1977, flew past Jupiter and Saturn, took the Pale Blue Dot picture in 1990, and reached interstellar space in 2012.

pages.title: Voyager 1's journey

items.name: Jupiter
items.text: Volcanoes on Io and a ring.

items.name: Pale Blue Dot
items.text: A last look back at home.

pages.say: In almost fifty years, Voyager 1 has visited two giant planets, looked back at Earth, and travelled farther than anything we have ever built.

pages.title: What Voyager taught us

items.name: Planet slingshots
items.text: Gravity assists from planets save years of travel. Many missions use them today.

items.name: Volcano worlds
items.text: Io showed that moons can be hot and active, not just cold, dead rocks.

items.name: Hidden oceans
items.text: Voyager's photos of Europa gave the first clues of an ocean under the ice.

items.name: The Sun's bubble
items.text: The Voyagers are the only spacecraft that have flown out through the edge of the heliosphere.

pages.say: Voyager taught us about planet slingshots, volcanic moons, hidden oceans, and the edge of the Sun's bubble.

complete.title: Chapter 5 complete!
lines: You found the launch window and made the Golden Record.
You photographed Jupiter and discovered a volcano on Io.
You coloured in Saturn and kept in touch across the solar system.
You found Earth, reached interstellar space and fixed Voyager from far away.
complete.guide: Incredible, star sailor! Next, let's land on Mars and explore it with NASA's robot rovers.
